title: Done or not yet
goal: The toughest unit in this module. Estonian marks whether an action is **finished or not** in the ending of the noun — a job English gives to verb forms like "am reading" and "have read".
bekal: choose between the genitive and the partitive for the object of an action
use one rule that never fails: after a negative, always the partitive
recognize verbs that always take the partitive

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Raamatupoes
dialogs.intro: The Rahva Raamat bookstore in central Tallinn. Budi is looking for a textbook.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Hello! I'm looking for a book.

lines.speaker: Müüja:
lines.id: Here you are, this one is good.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thank you. I'll buy this book.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jah, ma märkasin ka. Mis vahe on?
lines.id: Yes, I noticed too. What's the difference?
lines.literal: yes, I noticed-I too. what difference is-it?

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: "Otsin raamatut" — sa alles otsid. "Ostan raamatu" — asi saab tehtud.
lines.id: "Otsin raamatut" — you're still looking. "Ostan raamatu" — the deal is done.
lines.literal: "look-for-I book-part" — you still look-for-you. "buy-I book-gen" — thing gets done.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: So what matters is whether it's finished?

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Just. Indoneesia keeles sa ütled "sedang" ja "sudah", eks?
lines.id: Exactly. In Indonesian you say "sedang" and "sudah", right?
lines.literal: exactly. Indonesian language-in you say-you "sedang" and "sudah", right?

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Sama mõte. Meie paneme selle sõna lõppu, teie eraldi sõnasse.
lines.id: Same idea. We put it at the end of the word; you use a separate word.
lines.literal: same thought. we put-we it-gen word-gen end-to, you separate word-to.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Ja üks reegel on lihtne: eituse järel alati -t.
lines.id: And one easy rule: after a negative, always -t.
lines.literal: and one rule is-it easy: negative-gen after always -t.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Siis ma tean vähemalt ühe kindla reegli.
lines.id: Then I know at least one sure rule.
lines.literal: then I know-I at-least one-gen sure-gen rule-gen.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Ja kui kahtled — kasuta -t. Enamasti õige.
lines.id: And when in doubt — use -t. It's usually right.
lines.literal: and if doubt-you — use -t. mostly correct.

notes: ⚠️ **This is the core idea of the unit, and it's worth reading twice.** English marks whether an action is finished with the verb: *I'm reading* the book, *I've read* the book, *I read it through*. Estonian marks exactly the same thing by **changing the ending of the noun**. Same meaning; it just lives in a different place — exactly what happened with prepositions in unit 2.
**Ma otsin raamatut** — the action is in progress, no result yet. **Partitive**. **Ma ostan raamatu** — the action is complete; one whole book changes hands. **Genitive**.
**Millist raamatut?** — "which book?" Notice the question word is partitive too, because the noun is. Adjectives and demonstratives **always** copy the form of their noun; more on this in unit 14.
**Selle raamatu** — "this book". *See* becomes *selle* in the genitive, just like an ordinary noun. Its partitive is *seda*: *ma ei taha seda* (I don't want that).

grammars.title: Three forms, and when to use each
body: The object of an action can appear in three forms. The last column tells you when.
after: Compare the first two rows with English: *ma loen raamatut* = "I **am reading** a book"; *ma loen raamatu läbi* = "I **finish reading** the book". The word *läbi* (through, finished) makes it clearer, but the *-u* ending alone already carries that meaning.

⚠️ The third row is often forgotten: in **commands**, the object goes back to the nominative. *Osta raamat!* (Buy the book!), *Tee töö ära!* (Finish the job!). But if the command is negative, the partitive comes back: *Ära osta raamatut!*
The genitive used as an object is often called the "total object". The name doesn't matter; what matters is the picture — **the whole thing gets dealt with**.

grammars.title: Five situations that always take the partitive
body: If you memorize just one thing from this unit, make it this table. None of these five rows has exceptions at A1.

head: Situation
Example
Meaning
rows: I have a lot of work.

after: **The first row is the most valuable rule in this whole module.** After *ei* or *ära*, the object is **always** partitive — no exceptions, no conditions, no need to think about whether it's finished. If you remember only one thing, remember this.
You've been using the third row since unit 5 without knowing its name: *kohvi*, *teed*, *vett*, *piima*. Now you know why.
You've also used the fourth row since unit 4: *kaks eurot*, *kolm last*, *viis raamatut*. Note the noun stays singular after a number — only the ending is new.

sections.title: Verbs that always want the partitive

blocks.text: Some verbs can never naturally be "finished" — you can't finish loving or finish waiting. Such verbs **always** take the partitive, whatever the situation. The ten most common:

blocks.title: Partitive pronouns — used every day
items: *Ma armastan sind.* — I love you. *Ta tunneb mind.* — He/she knows me.
⚠️ *Teid* is used for "you" plural **and** for polite "you": *Ma tänan teid.* — Thank you (polite).
These forms are irregular and very common. Memorize all six now; you'll use them more often than any table in this unit.

blocks.text: Read each row aloud, pair by pair. The difference in the ending is small; the difference in meaning is big.

head: Not finished
Meaning
Finished
Meaning
rows: I read the book to the end.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Notice the small words in the third column: *läbi*, *ära*, *valmis*. Estonian often adds them to stress completion — they work just like English "up", "through" and "off" in *eat up*, *read through*, *finish off*. If you use one, the object is almost certainly genitive.

blocks.title: The order decides — use this when in doubt
items: **1.** Is the sentence negative? → **partitive**. Stop here; there's no other step.
**2.** Is the thing uncountable — a liquid, a material, time? → **partitive**.
**3.** Is there a number above one, or *palju*/*vähe*? → **partitive**.
**4.** Is the verb on the list of ten above? → **partitive**.

exercises.prompt: Choose the right form: genitive or partitive.
Make these sentences negative. Remember: after ei, always the partitive.
Put the words in the right order.

answers.0: raamatu — raamatut — raamatut — vett — piletit — sind
answers.1: Ma ei osta raamatut. — Ma ei söö õuna. — Ta ei loe kirja. — Me ei võta piletit. — Ma ei tea seda. — Nad ei ehita maja.
answers.2: Ma otsin raamatut. — Ma ostan selle raamatu. — Ma ei osta raamatut. — Ma ootan bussi. — Ma armastan sind. — Ma joon vett.
answers.3: Ma otsin raamatut. — Ma ostan selle raamatu. — Ma ei osta raamatut. — Ma ootan bussi. — Ma loen raamatu läbi.
